title: Eastern Europe
wiki_lead:
Eastern Europe is a subregion of the European continent. As a largely ambiguous term, it has a wide range of geopolitical, geographical, ethnic, cultural and socio-economic connotations. Its eastern boundary is conventionally drawn along the Ural Mountains, while its western boundary is defined in many different ways and has shifted over time. Narrow definitions, in which Central and Southeast Europe are counted as separate regions, include Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. Broader definitions also include Moldova and Romania and some or all of the Balkans, though generally not Greece or East Thrace, and sometimes the Baltic states, the Visegrád Group countries and the Caucasus. Russia, by far the largest country in the world, is also the largest in the region.
The main socio-cultural characteristics of Eastern Europe have historically been defined largely by the traditions of the Slavs and by the influence of Eastern Christianity as it developed through the Eastern Roman Empire. The Cold War created another definition, in which "Eastern Europe" meant the communist states of the Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc, separated from the West by the Iron Curtain.
The term is sometimes considered pejorative, through stereotypes of Eastern Europe as poorer and less developed than Western Europe, and the term Central and Eastern Europe is sometimes used as a more neutral grouping.
The region's history was shaped by the migrations of the Slavs in the 6th and 7th centuries, the Christianization of its peoples from both Rome and Constantinople, the Mongol invasions, and the rule of the Ottoman, Habsburg and Russian empires and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. After the First World War a series of new or restored states emerged, most of which were overrun by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union during the Second World War, when much of the region became a battlefield and the main site of the Holocaust. From 1945 to 1989 most of the region was under communist rule, and after the Revolutions of 1989 many of its countries joined NATO and the European Union.
Much of the region lies on the East European Plain, which is drained by long rivers such as the Volga, the longest in Europe, the Dnieper and the Danube, and its climate becomes more continental towards the east. Most of its states are parliamentary or semi-presidential republics, and eleven of them belong to the European Union, while Russia and Belarus give their presidents wide powers and were classed by Freedom House as consolidated authoritarian regimes. Since joining the EU several countries have moved closer to its average income per person, while Russia's economy relies heavily on the export of fossil fuels. Large-scale emigration and low fertility have reduced the population of many countries since 1990. The region's cultural traditions include Orthodox icon painting, the literature of writers such as Alexander Pushkin and Adam Mickiewicz, the music of Frédéric Chopin and scientific work such as Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table.

Eastern Europe is a subregion of the European continent. As a largely ambiguous term, it has a wide range of geopolitical, geographical, ethnic, cultural and socio-economic connotations. Its eastern boundary is conventionally drawn along the Ural Mountains, while its western boundary is defined in many different ways and has shifted over time. Narrow definitions, in which Central and Southeast Europe are counted as separate regions, include Belarus, Russia and Ukraine. Broader definitions also include Moldova and Romania and some or all of the Balkans, though generally not Greece or East Thrace, and sometimes the Baltic states, the Visegrád Group countries and the Caucasus. Russia, by far the largest country in the world, is also the largest in the region.
The main socio-cultural characteristics of Eastern Europe have historically been defined largely by the traditions of the Slavs and by the influence of Eastern Christianity as it developed through the Eastern Roman Empire. The Cold War created another definition, in which "Eastern Europe" meant the communist states of the Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc, separated from the West by the Iron Curtain.
The term is sometimes considered pejorative, through stereotypes of Eastern Europe as poorer and less developed than Western Europe, and the term Central and Eastern Europe is sometimes used as a more neutral grouping.
The region's history was shaped by the migrations of the Slavs in the 6th and 7th centuries, the Christianization of its peoples from both Rome and Constantinople, the Mongol invasions, and the rule of the Ottoman, Habsburg and Russian empires and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth. After the First World War a series of new or restored states emerged, most of which were overrun by Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union during the Second World War, when much of the region became a battlefield and the main site of the Holocaust. From 1945 to 1989 most of the region was under communist rule, and after the Revolutions of 1989 many of its countries joined NATO and the European Union.
Much of the region lies on the East European Plain, which is drained by long rivers such as the Volga, the longest in Europe, the Dnieper and the Danube, and its climate becomes more continental towards the east. Most of its states are parliamentary or semi-presidential republics, and eleven of them belong to the European Union, while Russia and Belarus give their presidents wide powers and were classed by Freedom House as consolidated authoritarian regimes. Since joining the EU several countries have moved closer to its average income per person, while Russia's economy relies heavily on the export of fossil fuels. Large-scale emigration and low fertility have reduced the population of many countries since 1990. The region's cultural traditions include Orthodox icon painting, the literature of writers such as Alexander Pushkin and Adam Mickiewicz, the music of Frédéric Chopin and scientific work such as Dmitri Mendeleev's periodic table.


Definitions

Several definitions of Eastern Europe exist in the early 21st century, but they often lack precision and may be anachronistic. The term has been called "fuzzy", an idea that is continually being redefined. The historian Larry Wolff has argued that the idea of "Eastern Europe" was created in the 18th century by thinkers of the Enlightenment, who cultivated an image of its backwardness, and the literary scholar Thomas Grob traces it primarily to the French Enlightenment. In a paper for the United Nations Group of Experts on Geographical Names, the geographer Peter Jordan wrote that "every assessment of spatial identities is essentially a social and cultural construct".


History of the concept

Ancient Greek geographers believed that Europe and Asia were separated by a river, the Tanais, which they thought flowed south from the Arctic into the Sea of Azov. Renaissance geographers still relied on these ancient ideas, with the Tanais, identified with the Don, dividing Europe from Asia, until Maciej Miechowita and Sigismund von Herberstein revised this view in their writings on Muscovy. Within Europe, the main cultural and political division for centuries ran between north and south. According to the historian Frithjof Benjamin Schenk, the model of a "civilized" South and a "barbarian" North lost its predominance only at the end of the 18th and the beginning of the 19th centuries, and until then British, French and German textbooks presented Russia mainly as a "Northern" country.
The term "Eastern Europe" appeared in geographical writing in the early 18th century, as in the title of a 1730 travel account by the Swedish officer Philip Johan von Strahlenberg, who had been in Siberia as a Russian prisoner of war. According to the geographer Mark Bassin, the Russian historian Vasily Tatishchev was the first to propose, in the 1730s, that the Ural Mountains replace the Tanais as the boundary between Europe and Asia, placing the core Russian lands in Europe and Siberia in Asia. Wolff describes a reorientation from the earlier "Northern" and "Southern" Europe by philosophes who viewed the continent from Paris, and Grob notes that Voltaire wrote of an Orient de l'Europe, a zone geographically in Europe that had not yet benefited from the new philosophy. After the Congress of Vienna, Conrad Malte-Brun counted only Russia and Poland as Europe orientale and Adriano Balbi proposed a two-part division into western and eastern Europe, while Russia moved on Europe's mental maps from the "North" to the "East".
In 1923 the Polish historian Oskar Halecki argued at the International Congress of Historical Sciences in Brussels that Eastern Europe was a subdivided region, much of which had always belonged culturally to Western civilization. After 1945 the term acquired a mainly political meaning in Western languages. In The Limits and Divisions of European History (1950) Halecki divided medieval and modern Europe into western, central and eastern regions, with a "West-Central" and an "East-Central" half in the middle. The Hungarian historian Jenő Szűcs, in his essay Sketch on the Three Regions of Europe (1983), distinguished Western Europe, East-Central Europe and an Eastern Europe largely identified with Russia. In 1984 the Czech writer Milan Kundera wrote of the "tragedy of Central Europe", setting Czechs, Poles and Hungarians apart from Russia and the Soviet Union. According to Diana Mishkova, Maria Todorova's Imagining the Balkans (1997) offered a "Balkanist" critique of the Balkans as an image in the Western mind, though Todorova also saw real features of the region in the Ottoman legacy.


Geographical

Europe's eastern boundary is conventionally drawn along the Ural Mountains, but it does not mark a cultural, political or economic divide, and it has long been debated. Kazakhstan, which lies mainly in Central Asia, has a small portion west of the Ural River in the easternmost part of Europe.
In the west there is no geographical boundary between Eastern and Western Europe. The line is drawn on historical, religious and cultural grounds and has moved over time, so that Prague, Ljubljana and Zagreb are often thought of as "eastern" although they lie further west than Vienna.
For statistical purposes the United Nations counts Belarus, Bulgaria, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Moldova, Poland, Romania, Russia, Slovakia and Ukraine as Eastern Europe and places Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania in Northern Europe, noting that its groupings are made "for statistical convenience".


Religious and cultural influence

After the East–West Schism of 1054, significant parts of Eastern Europe developed cultural unity and resistance to Catholic Western and Central Europe within the framework of the Eastern Orthodox Church, Church Slavonic language and the Cyrillic alphabet.
A large section of Eastern Europe is formed by countries with dominant Orthodox churches, like Belarus, Bulgaria, Cyprus, Georgia, Greece, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Romania, Russia, Serbia, and Ukraine, for instance, as well as Armenia, which is predominantly Armenian Apostolic. The Eastern Orthodox Church has played a prominent role in the history and culture of Eastern and Southeastern Europe. Eastern Catholic Churches, which keep Eastern rites but are in communion with Rome, became significant after the Union of Brest in 1596, when all but two of the Ukrainian Orthodox bishops in the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth accepted the primacy of the pope, although smaller groups had united with Rome earlier.
The schism refers to the historical break of communion and theology between the Eastern (Orthodox) and Western (Catholic) churches. Later developments meant that the divide was no longer solely between Catholic and Orthodox churches. From the 16th century, both Western and Eastern forms of Protestantism began to emerge in Europe.
Since the Great Schism of 1054, Europe has been divided between Catholic (and later additionally Protestant) churches in the West, and the Eastern Orthodox Christian churches in the east. The religious cleavage causes Eastern Orthodox countries to be often associated with Eastern Europe. This divide is an imperfect guide, however. Greece, for example, is overwhelmingly Orthodox, but the United Nations classes it as part of Southern Europe. The historian Ian Armour notes that use of the Cyrillic alphabet is not a strict marker of Eastern Europe either, since the Latin alphabet is used from Croatia to Poland.


Cold War usage

During the Cold War, "Eastern Europe" was used more or less as a synonym for the Soviet-dominated Eastern Bloc and the Warsaw Pact. This usage still shapes how the term is understood, although historians and social scientists generally regard definitions based on it as outdated.


EuroVoc

EuroVoc, a multilingual thesaurus maintained by the Publications Office of the European Union, groups Albania, Belarus, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Kosovo, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Poland, Romania, Russia, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia and Ukraine as "Central and Eastern Europe", together with a subgroup of Caucasus countries. Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania are not part of this group.


Regional classifications
In broadest definition, the countries are Albania, Armenia, Azerbaijan, Belarus, Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bulgaria, Croatia, the Czech Republic, Estonia, Hungary, Kosovo, Latvia, Lithuania, Moldova, Montenegro, North Macedonia, Poland, Romania, Russia, Serbia, Slovakia, Slovenia, Ukraine and, in rare cases, Greece, which is more commonly classified differently, albeit less commonly placed in Eastern Europe, all of which can be classified into 6 categories. 
Despite being predominantly located in West Asia, the South Caucasus nations of Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia are often categorized as part of Eastern Europe.


Baltic states

Estonia, Latvia and Lithuania, known together as the Baltic states, lie in north-eastern Europe on the eastern shore of the Baltic Sea. The United Nations places them in Northern Europe, and EuroVoc does not include them in its Central and Eastern European group. They are sometimes counted as part of Central Europe instead.

Caucasus states

The South Caucasus nations of Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia are included in definitions or histories of Eastern Europe. They are located in the transition zone of Eastern Europe and Western Asia. They participate in the European Union's Eastern Partnership program, the Euronest Parliamentary Assembly, and are members of the Council of Europe, which specifies that all three have political and cultural connections to Europe. In January 2002, the European Parliament noted that Armenia, Azerbaijan, and Georgia may enter the EU in the future. Georgia and Armenia are seeking EU membership, with Georgia also seeking NATO membership alongside.

grok_lead: Eastern Europe constitutes a subregion of the European continent, delineated by the United Nations geoscheme as comprising Belarus, Bulgaria, Czechia, Hungary, Poland, the Republic of Moldova, Romania, the Russian Federation, Slovakia, and Ukraine. This area spans diverse geographical features, including the vast Eastern European Plain, the Carpathian Mountains, and coastlines along the Baltic, Black, and Caspian Seas, fostering a range of climates from temperate to continental. Historically, the region has been shaped by successive imperial dominions, including the Russian Empire, Austro-Hungarian Empire, and Ottoman Empire, culminating in post-World War II subjugation under Soviet control, where communist governments imposed centralized planning and suppressed political dissent across the Eastern Bloc. The Iron Curtain demarcation isolated these states from Western Europe, enforcing ideological conformity until the revolutions of 1989 triggered the collapse of communist regimes and the dissolution of the Soviet Union in 1991. In the contemporary era, Eastern European nations exhibit marked variation in political trajectories and economic performance, with severalâsuch as Poland, Czechia, Hungary, Slovakia, Romania, and Bulgaria âintegrating into the European Union and NATO, driving market-oriented reforms that yielded substantial GDP growth in outperformers like Poland, while others grapple with authoritarian consolidation in Belarus and ongoing conflict with Russian forces in Ukraine. Culturally, the region is characterized by Slavic linguistic dominance, a blend of Eastern Orthodox and Roman Catholic traditions, and resilient national identities forged through centuries of external pressures, contributing to both internal ethnic tensions and a collective emphasis on sovereignty amid geopolitical strains.
